# Line Graphs {#ggplot2-line-graph}

## Introduction

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this chart

Line graphs show change over an ordered axis, usually time; slope is the message.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

Unsorted or gappy x values draw zigzag lines; sort by x and handle missing periods explicitly.
:::

In this chapter, we will learn to:

- build 
    - simple line chart
    - grouped line chart
- map aesthetics to variables
- modify line
    - color
    - type
    - size

```{r line, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```

## Case Study

We will use `EuStockMarkets`, a data set that ships with R. It records the
daily closing prices of four European stock indices — DAX (Germany), SMI
(Switzerland), CAC (France) and FTSE (United Kingdom) — from mid-1991 to
mid-1998. See `?EuStockMarkets` for details and the source.

### Data

```{r import200, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
stocks <- as.data.frame(EuStockMarkets)
stocks$year <- as.numeric(time(EuStockMarkets))
head(stocks)
```

`year` is the decimal year recorded by `time()`, so `1991.5` is mid-1991.

## Line Chart

To create a line chart, use `geom_line()`. In the below example, we examine the
DAX index over the period.

```{r line100, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line()
```

### Line Color

To modify the color of the line, use the `color` argument and supply it a valid
color name. In the below example, we modify the color of the line to `'blue'`. 
Remember that the `color` argument should be outside `aes()`.

```{r line1, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(color = 'blue')
```

### Line Type

The line type can be modified using the `linetype` argument. It can take 7 different
values. You can specify the line type either using numbers or words as shown below:

- 0 : blank
- 1 : solid
- 2 : dashed
- 3 : dotted
- 4 : dotdash
- 5 : longdash
- 6 : twodash

Let us modify the line type to dashed style by supplying the value `2` to the
`linetype` argument.

```{r line2, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(linetype = 2)
```

The above example can be recreated by supplying the value `'dashed'` instead 
of `2`.

```{r line3, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(linetype = 'dashed')
```

### Line Size

The width of the line can be modified using the `linewidth` argument. It can take
any value above 0 as input.

```{r line4, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 2)
```

## Multiple Lines

### Modify Data

Now let us map the aesthetics to the variables. The data used in the above 
example cannot be used as we need a variable with index names. We will use 
`pivot_longer()` function from the `tidyr` package to reshape the data.

```{r line5, fig.align='center'}
stocks2 <- stocks |>
  select(year, DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = -year, names_to = "index", values_to = "price")

head(stocks2)
```

In the original data, to plot the price trend of multiple indices we will have
to use `geom_line()` multiple times. But in the reshaped data, we have the 
index names as one of the variables and this can be used along with the 
`group` argument to plot data of multiple indices with a single line of code 
as shown below. By mapping index to the `group` argument, we have plotted 
data of all indices.

```{r line6, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line()
```

In the above plot, we cannot distinguish between the lines and there is no way
to identify which line represents which index. To make it easier to identify
the trend of different indices, let us map the `color` argument to the 
variable index as shown below. Now, each index will be represented by line 
of different color.

```{r line7, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = index))
```

We can map `linetype` argument to index as well. In this case, each index
will be represented by a different line type.

```{r line8, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = index))
```

We can map the width of the line to the variable index as well. But in this 
case, the plot does not look either elegant or intuitive. 

```{r line9, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = index))
```

Remember that in all the above cases, we mapped the arguments to a variable 
inside `aes()`.

## Exercises

1. Draw the `unemploy` series from `economics` over `date` with `linewidth = 1`.
2. Reshape `unemploy` + `uempmed` to long format and draw both series distinguished by color.
3. Rewrite the plot with a message-first title and units on the y axis.
